document.title: Comments of Consumers' Research re the large loads co-located at generation facilities

COMMENT OF CONSUMERS’ RESEARCH 
Pursuant to the Commission’s Order entered on February 20, 2025, at Docket Nos. EL25-
49-000 et al., Intervenor Consumers’ Research submits the following comment responding to the 
filings in this docket and addressing four key principles that should guide the Commission’s 
decision making when considering how to protect consumers and ensure reliable and affordable 
electricity in the context of large loads co-located at generating facilities. 
Consumers’ Research is an independent educational 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization 
whose mission is to increase the knowledge and understanding of issues, policies, products, and 
services of concern to consumers and to promote the freedom to act on that knowledge and 
understanding.1  The cost and reliability of energy is a critical issue for the organization because 
it affects not only household utility bills but also the cost of energy that is factored into every good 
and service that consumers purchase.  
First, retail customers should not subsidize the costs of co-location of large loads. 
Consumers’ Research agrees with PJM that “participants involved in co-location arrangements 
 
1 See https://consumersresearch.org/

2 
should pay the costs of any grid services they consume and the arrangements must be reliable and 
operationally manageable.” See PJM Answer at 4. And it is undisputed that “many co-located load 
configurations utilize grid support and consume ancillary services (including, for example, 
frequency regulation, black start service, and reactive service).” Id. 
To avoid improper subsidization, the Commission and regional transmission organizations 
should consider both direct and indirect costs, including the following: infrastructure that is built 
to power the co-located load itself; existing and new or upgraded infrastructure, including 
generators and transmission, that is ostensibly for the benefit of regular consumers but that is made 
necessary by the allocation of existing base-load power to the co-located load; developments to 
ensure reliability and resource adequacy, including ancillary developments like backups and black 
start, that are necessary because of the co-located load’s impact on reliability; grid support that 
enables the co-located load to receive reliable power in case of the connected generator’s failure 
or shortfall; and potential rate increases resulting from decreased supply caused by co-location. In 
consideration of this, a co-located load’s access to, dependence on, and use of grid-supplied energy 
must be thoroughly accounted for when forming the co-located load’s rate structure.  
Second, retail customers should not bear the risks of co-location. The risks of co-location 
should not be distributed to or socialized among regular consumers. Co-location may require large 
upfront costs for infrastructure, and there is a risk that those costs will not be recovered (e.g., if the 
company that obtained the co-location fails). Another risk of co-location is that the co-located load 
could obtain the first right of access to reliable, dispatchable power, while regular consumers are 
left with less reliable resources like wind and solar. 
To protect regular consumers from the risks of co-location, including the risk of stranded 
assets, co-located loads could be required to do the following as a precondition to the risks: make

3 
long-term financial commitments that will insure against risks; agree to a take-or-pay clause that 
applies over a defined period of time; and paying for the development of additional reliable power 
generation to ensure that regular consumers maintain the same level of generation from reliable 
sources as they did before the co-location. 
Third, co-location should not be allowed to undermine dispatchable power—including by 
serving as an alternative to using existing dispatchable, generating sources that will otherwise 
retire. According to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), many states 
are now at risk of suffering critical shortfalls in electric power. The amount of money at issue to 
address this shortfall is enormous: construction costs alone are estimated to be in the trillions,2 and 
that does not even account for the indirect costs to consumers and the economy from bad policy 
choices. Early retirement and non-repair of dispatchable generating assets is shortening their useful 
lifespans, and there is a general failure to build new dispatchable generating assets. As Chair 
Christie stated, “I have repeatedly warned that America is facing a reliability crisis driven by the 
dangerous pace of retirements of dispatchable generation units and failure to build sufficient new 
generation.”3 It is important that co-location of certain resources not occur in a way that 
exacerbates (or fails to ameliorate) the reliability crisis facing many states. 
FERC should therefore consider several possible policies. For example, parties engaged in 
co-location arrangements could be required to maintain a specified reserve capacity of 
dispatchable power for use by ratepayers that are not part of the co-location. This could help to 
 
2 BloombergNEF estimated that the cost of the grid overhaul globally could be $21 trillion 
between 2020-2035. https://www.ft.com/content/bf1b788a-f366-4637-9ae4-08dbc0bd90fa. The 
U.S. portion of that may be $2.5 trillion according to an IEA report. 
https://markets.businessinsider.com/news/stocks/grid-upgrades-estimated-to-cost-over-25-
trillion-by-2035-1032726083 
3 https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/president-trump-names-mark-christie-chairman-ferc

4 
ensure that generators and utilities, in addition to companies seeking to co-locate, are properly 
incentivized to promote dispatchable power.  
It is also critical that co-location not be allowed unless the parties involved, including the 
generator and the company seeking the co-location, have no targets or commitments for net zero 
or any related low-carbon goals. Co-located loads often demand 24/7 dispatchable power, so they 
should not be allowed to misleadingly claim that they are lowering their emissions by co-locating 
to a “clean” facility while simultaneously creating risks to existing dispatchable generation that is 
supplied to the grid. Net-zero commitments and related targets harm consumers by artificially 
weakening the market for dispatchable power.  
In contrast, if a co-located load plans to connect a new generator that provides dispatchable 
power (e.g., a new fossil-fuel-powered generator) and will also increase grid reliability overall 
(rather than decrease it), then FERC should consider policies that allow that new generation to 
move ahead in the interconnection queue, in front of projects for non-dispatchable resources. 
Time-savings incentives may be important in this context, as one of the reasons that companies 
seek co-location is to avoid delays and start operating profitably as quickly as possible. Allowing 
dispatchable generation (that benefits consumers generally) to move forward in the queue is 
consistent with solving a problem identified by Interior Secretary Burgum, who identified the 
problem of the 2,600 GW of wind, solar and storage sitting in the interconnection queues as a 
major energy imbalance that could lead to brownouts or blackouts.4  And the Commission has 
adopted a rule allowing dispatchable generation to get priority in the queue.5  
 
4 https://www.rtoinsider.com/95864-burgum-criticizes-ferc-queues-renewables/  
5 https://medium.com/@kennedymaize/ferc-approves-line-jumping-pjm-connections-
32561997e8bd

5 
Fourth, co-location arrangements should be transparent to the public. Companies seeking 
co-location may try to benefit from special contracts that are not open to the public. Transparency 
will also help protect consumers from the risk that their power infrastructure will be built up, at 
the consumers’ long-term expense, for a co-location that eventually falls through when a company 
decides to withdraw its interconnection request and instead follow through on a duplicative request 
that it made somewhere else. Companies seeking co-location should also be required to disclose 
information about the extent and nature of any on-site backup generating facilities. 
Thank you for considering the comments of Consumers’ Research on this important issue. 
Ultimately, the key consideration must be promoting affordable and reliable electricity to 
consumers. The foregoing principles will help achieve that goal. 
Dated: April 23, 2025  
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Will Hild
